A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RATE research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 Section 5 and Appendix B report original reward-model evaluations, distribution-shift experiments, and comparisons of single and double rewrites.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds a controlled vowel/typo experiment in Section 5.1, with further results and examples in Appendices C–E.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same attribute flip, reverse rewrite, reward differences, and weighted ATT/ATU combination. The revised notation, stronger theoretical claim, and additional experiments do not establish a change to the proposed estimation procedure.

E1.justification: IMDB, ELI5, HelpSteer, and HH-RLHF remain covered, including the existing length, sentiment, complexity, and helpfulness evaluations. v2 adds the target attribute 'starts with a vowel' on IMDB under deliberately introduced typos, providing a distinct corruption scenario.

E2.justification: v1 Figure 3 compares RATE with the naive estimator in the IMDB/DistilBERT and HelpSteer/ArmoRM distribution-shift experiments. v2 Figures 4 and 6 add the single-rewrite comparator to those experiments. Single rewriting already appeared elsewhere in v1; the three principal reward models remain the same.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a controlled sweep from 0% to 30% typos in vowel-starting reviews. The retained distribution-shift plots change their reported scale from 'Reward' to 'Effect Size,' and combined-dataset length/sentiment summaries replace separate appendix summaries. The existing resampling-count tables and 512-token exclusion remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the diagnostic analysis of error cancellation: its new vowel/typo stress test directly examines when single rewriting becomes biased, while existing distribution-shift tests gain single-rewrite controls. Conversely, the ELI5 reward-distribution diagnostic in v1 Figure 4 disappears; its HH-RLHF counterpart survives as v2 Figure 2.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals and explain that normal approximations are used because of large sample sizes. Neither introduces seed counts, repeated-run reporting, significance tests, or a different uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 Figure 3 adds results showing RATE near zero as typo frequency increases, while naive and single-rewrite estimates become increasingly negative. Reported real-model summaries also change: RATE sentiment estimates lie below naive estimates in v1 Figure 2 but above them in v2 Figure 5. Revised scales and aggregation preclude interpreting these as same-setting performance gains. The reward tuples in v1 Tables 8–12 remain unchanged in v2 Tables 9–13.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 strengthens ordinary consistency to root-n consistency and explicitly introduces bounded rewards, i.i.d. sampling, and nonzero treatment-group probabilities. Appendix B supplies a new rate argument. v2 also corrects the single-rewrite expression and formal rewrite transition to flip the target attribute. These revise the mathematical substance while retaining the estimator.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain causal measurement of reward-model attribute sensitivity, correction of imperfect rewrites through double rewriting, validity under assumptions, and empirical importance relative to confounded evaluations. The revised title and contribution list emphasize explainability without materially redefining these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit limitations concerning subjective counterfactual validation and the uncertain connection between reward sensitivity and downstream aligned-LLM behavior. It removes v1's warnings about omitting the prompt during rewriting and safety-tuned models resisting unhelpful rewrites, along with discussions of dynamic benchmarking and prompt-rewriting extensions.

D1.justification: v2 adds documentation of the typo intervention and complete prompt/response/rewrite examples in Appendix E.4. However, the explicit disclosure that the implemented rewriter ignores the original prompt is lost; the PDFs do not establish that this implementation changed. The GPT-4o version, generation costs, existing rewrite prompts, and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds comparisons with Jiang et al. on reward-model explanations and Bhattacharjee et al. on counterfactual generation, plus references including Imbens and Rubin, Pan, and Tien. Discussions and citations including Gleave, Eisenstein, and Kaushik are removed. The broader positioning within causal text analysis and LLM-generated counterfactuals remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, theoretical exposition, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Semi-synthetic experiments now precede real-model evaluations, conclusion and discussion are combined, and reproducibility information and experimental material are reorganized into Appendices A–E.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout. Figures are redrawn, reordered, split, or consolidated; the vowel/typo experiment adds a figure and example table. Existing prompt and example tables move, additional sample tables appear, and full examples receive a separate appendix presentation.

improvement.justification: The targeted typo experiment and added single-rewrite controls improve the empirical justification for double rewriting beyond v1's demonstrations of differing estimates. Fuller examples and explicit downstream limitations also improve scrutiny. These gains are qualified: the near-zero ground truth remains assumed, the prompt-omission disclosure is lost, and Appendix B's new ATE rate derivation omits fluctuations in treatment-group weights. The net improvement is therefore limited.
